decisions.reason: Report grounds the diagnosis in the session log and env-state: the session and its tool worker run inside the host process npm was replacing, the host dies first, the GUI drops, and the tool call's final outcome stays unknown. It frames the failure as structural, not a network fluke, and explicitly avoids claiming every in-place upgrade must crash.

Explains from env-state.txt that package content exists while dsh/dsh.cmd are missing and dsh.ps1 is stale, so PATH resolution fails and content presence does not prove a complete install; it ties the manually swapped tree to the broken shim state and rejects hand-swapping/hand-made shims as the fix.

Grounds the remedy in repair-notes.md: rerun npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.2-rc.1 from outside the dead host so npm regenerates the shims, verified by dsh --version equal to rc.1; also accounts for aligning the source checkout to the rc.1 tag with no unrelated edits, and keeps the recorded repair separate from candidate actions.

The report says the agent must recognize it runs on the upgrade target and refuse to execute the global install in that session; the handed-off procedure stops the host before the exact-version pinned install, then restarts, refreshes the browser and verifies. It labels stop-host-first and version pinning as established rules and the refusal-from-inside-target as the new self-host rule, and the external shell is a fresh terminal rather than a dependent tool of the dying host.

Proposes a guard that resolves the install target and compares it to its own runtime/worker path, refusing self-upgrade-shaped calls. Uses the alpha.5→rc.1 version-only diff to conclude no plugin re-migration is needed, and its checklist covers displayed version markers, fresh shims, actual plugin loading after restart/refresh, and backup cleanup only after verification — all specific to the supplied tags with no code changes.

caps.reason: The report's final advice explicitly rejects executing or retrying the upgrade from inside the target host and requires the host be stopped before npm runs; the in-session install appears only as the analyzed failure.
The final fix is the formal external pinned install; manual directory swaps and hand-made shims are described only as the user's failed attempt and are explicitly rejected.
